newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Ifo says German '97 GDP to grow by 2-2.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ifo says German '97 GDP to grow by 2-2.5 pct.

text.p: The Ifo economic research institute said on Thursday it expected German 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by between two and two and a half percent, driven mainly by exports.

Healthy exports, aided by a relatively soft deutschmark, was boosting foreign demand and should spark a pick-up in domestic demand over the year, Ifo said. But it noted there were risks to this scenario.
"As foreign orders figures show, exports will remain the driving force behind the German economy in 1997," Ifo President Karl-Heinrich Oppenlaender told Ifo's annual meeting.
The mark has fallen sharply versus the dollar this year, reducing the cost of German goods to foreign customers.
Oppenlaender said this decline had more than compensated for the mark's appreciation in early 1995.
"The conditions for contiuned economic recovery are favourable. All in all, we expect a rise in real GDP of between two to two and a half percent (in 1997)," he told the meeting.

But Germany's painfully high unemployment was unlikely to benefit from that growth this year, Oppenlaender said. Instead, the average number of unemployed will likely rise by more than 300,000 to 4.3 million in 1997 while the average number of those in work falls by 400,000 over the year.
While this upward trend in unemployment is forecast to turn next year, Oppenlaender said average unemployment will still be 4.2 million in 1998.
In 1998, Ifo forecasts GDP to rise to 2.75 percent but said this prediction took into account a number of favourable circumstances and was therefore, at the upper-end of the range.

"In particular, we have assumed (with this forecast) that European economic and monetary union (EMU), after Europe-wide savings measures, will start on time with a relatively large number of participants," he said.

While exports and foreign demand were picking up, Oppenlaender said weak domestic demand and Eastern Germany's struggling economic recovery presented a substantial problem for overall German progress.
"Seven years after reunification, the recovery process (in east Germany) has been interrupted," Oppenlaender said.
Despite higher levels of investment, insufficient competitiveness was keeping the region from achieving self-sustaining growth levels.
In 1997, per capita GDP in the East was likely to reach 55 percent of that in West Germany, he said.
